Reading a long document in overlapping windows often yields different results than processing it in a single pass due to the fundamental limitations of context windows and the loss of global coherence. When a model processes text in chunks, it only sees a local slice of the information. Even with overlapping windows to mitigate abrupt cutoffs, the model cannot simultaneously hold the entire narrative, argument structure, or distant dependencies in its active working memory.

Consequently, the model may prioritize information that appears early in a specific window while ignoring crucial context that exists in a previous or subsequent window. This leads to fragmented reasoning where local details are over-weighted relative to the global theme. Additionally, the model’s attention mechanism is constrained by the finite size of the input; it cannot effectively attend to tokens that are far outside the current window. In a single-pass approach, the model can integrate all evidence, resolve ambiguities using the full scope of the text, and maintain a consistent logical thread. In contrast, windowed reading forces the model to make provisional judgments based on incomplete data, which may be contradicted by later information. These local biases accumulate, resulting in an answer that reflects a patchwork of partial understandings rather than a holistic synthesis.
